name: Inca religion
info: Inca religion was the polytheist system of beliefs and rites of the Inca Empire, or Tawantinsuyu, which grew out of older Andean traditions and centred on the Sun god Inti, the creator Viracocha, sacred places called wak'a and the worship of royal ancestors.

facts.origin: the Andes, evolving from pre-Inca times into the religion of the Inca Empire, with its state cult centred on Cusco; many origin stories place the beginning of life at Lake Titicaca

facts.followers: none counted: Spanish authorities moved against the worship of the royal mummies from 1559, and Pachamama is still honoured in Bolivian indigenous belief

sections.origins:
The Inca religion was a group of beliefs and rites related to a mythological system that evolved from pre-Inca times into the Inca Empire, or Tawantinsuyu. Its followers were polytheists, with local, regional and pan-regional divinities, and faith showed itself in every part of life, work, festivals and ceremonies. The Incas took over and institutionalised the religious practices of older Andean societies, most notably the Wari, Chavín and Nazca cultures. Aspects of Andean religion reach beyond the empire's former borders to the Mapuches and Huilliches of southern Chile, which has raised the hypothesis of an earlier spread of Andean religion from Tiwanaku.

The Incas had a great number of origin stories, which historians and scholars find hard to sort out; they often contradict themselves, seeming to retell a story later to take in events that had since happened. Many place the beginning of life at Lake Titicaca. The stories show an attitude of change, in which the past could be altered to suit the present, so that newly met peoples and lands could be said to have been there from the beginning. They do not stand for the origin stories of other pre-Inca Andean peoples, of which there are many more versions. Many people thought that their founding ancestor had arisen from an exact spot, a paqarisqa.
sections.beliefs:
A theme of Inca mythology is the duality of the cosmos. Hanan pacha, the upper world, held the deities of the sun, moon, stars, rainbow and lightning; ukhu pacha and urin pacha were the realms of Pachamama, the earth mother, and of the ancestors and heroes of the Inca and other ayllus; kay pacha, where humans lived, lay between them. The condor stood for the upper world, the puma for the outer earth and the snake for the inner earth. In Andean thought, asymmetrical dualism holds that reality is built by different forces that need each other to be complete, one slightly stronger than the other. Camac is the life force that inhabits everything, living or dead, in different quantities, and places and objects with special energy were called wak'a: mountains, boulders, streams, battlefields, pottery believed to carry a deity.

Among the official deities were Viracocha, creator of humanity and everything else; Inti, the sun god, whose temple was the Coricancha, the Golden Enclosure; Illapa, who controlled weather, rain and lightning; Mamaquilla, Mother Moon and wife of Inti; Pachamama, the Earth Mother, protector of fields and crops; and Mama Cocha, Mother of Lakes. The Pleiades (Qollqa), mother of the stellar deities, marked the start of the agricultural year when they reappeared after 37 days unseen. Families sometimes kept household gods as small figures called chancas or conopas.
sections.texts:
No scriptures are recorded. Because of the Spanish conquest much direct evidence of Inca religion was lost, and modern historians rely heavily on colonial chronicles and on the archaeological remains of religious customs. The ritual duties of each shrine at Cusco were recorded on quipus, knotted string recording devices. Juan de Betanzos is cited for the Incas' turn to secrecy after the Spaniards arrived, and Garcilaso de la Vega for his sight of the embalmed kings at the house of Polo de Ondegardo.

One account of the origin has the creator god Wiraqocha Pachayachachic form giants at Lake Titicaca to see whether humans would work well at that size. Finding that they did not, he made them of his own size. These humans were hubristic and greedy and were turned to stone or other forms, some engulfed by stone or sea. The Creator then summoned a great flood to destroy all life except three men, who would later help create humans again. At a later point at Lake Titicaca he made the sun, moon and stars. The moon shone brighter than the sun, and the sun, filled with jealousy, threw ashes in her face to dim her. The Creator then spread out with two servants to call forth the people of every nation, from every mountain, crevice, cave and lake, before walking over the water into the west.
sections.spread:
Religious traditions in the Andes varied among the different ayllus. The Inca generally allowed, or even took in, the deities and heroes of the ayllus they conquered, but they also brought their own gods to those peoples by building them into law, for instance by requiring sacrifice. They tried to combine their deities with conquered ones in ways that raised the status of their own. Pachamama, worshipped long before the rise of the Inca, was integrated into Inca mythology and placed below the Moon, who the Inca believed ruled over all female gods.

The official tradition of the empire was the cult of the Sun, but locals were allowed to worship their existing beings. They did so through pilgrimages, offerings and other rites that let them keep to tradition while still providing the sacrifices and offerings due to the Sun god. Many of the local peoples believed that their founding ancestor had come out of a particular spot, a paqarisqa.

The state religion was administrative and concentrated in Cusco, where a complex calendar set the state's festivals, holy days and major ceremonies. The Incas built a highly centralised religious framework that regulated almost every aspect of civic and spiritual life within the empire.
sections.community:
Cusco's sacred geography held 328 huacas, objects, landmarks or shrines in and around the valley, arranged along 41 or 42 radial pathways called ceques that all began at the Coricancha. Ten royal kindred groups of Inca nobility, the panacas, served as the main priesthood in Cusco. They were responsible for the ancestral worship of dead emperors and the veneration of state deities, and were organised in two divisions of five, Hanan (Upper Cusco), north of the river, and Hurin (Lower Cusco), to the south. They took turns in ritual duties, offering sacrifices to the Sun, the Moon, Thunder, Viracocha and the Earth, the five powers that received most of the state's sacrifices.

The Inca calendar had 12 months of 30 days, each with a festival, and a five-day feast at the end. The year began in December with Qhapaq Raymi, the first and biggest festival, when boys went through their puberty rites. Inti Raymi, at the June solstice, honoured the Sun god and ended with the ruler first to plough the earth. In Qoya Raymi the Situa purified Cuzco of disease, with runners carrying ashes along the four roads out of the city.

Divination came before any action and nearly every rite was accompanied by sacrifices, usually maize beer, food or llamas, but occasionally virgins or children. Human sacrifice, usually of a child (qhapaq hucha) or a slave, is confirmed by archaeological remains on high mountain summits; in times of great trouble specially chosen children were taken up to freezing peaks and left, either plied with alcohol or in some cases strangled. The Incas are said to have thought it an honour to die as an offering.
sections.legacy:
Rulers were often mummified at death and worshipped within the palaces. Several times a year the mummies were seated in the order of their reigns in Cuzco's plaza, and in other months they were returned to their palaces and visited. They were seen as possessing agency, not really alive nor dead, and the ruling Inca was expected to seek their advice on important matters. Under Pachacutic seven past rulers were made into wawqis. Local leaders, the curacas, were preserved as mallki, and the queens, the Coya, were tied to the moon goddess Quilla. Not all mummies were honoured: Topa Inca Yupanqui's was burned and his bloodline killed for siding with Huascar in the civil war.

When the Spanish arrived, the Incas began to hide the bodies of the kings and worshipped more secretly. Polo de Ondegardo, appointed Corregidor of Cuzco in 1559, tried to stop what he saw as the Incas' idolatrous sins, found most of the mummified kings and sent them to the viceroy in Lima. They stayed in the Hospital of San Andrés for around 80 years before their whereabouts became unknown. Pachamama is still described as a source of fertility and abundance in Bolivian indigenous belief.

summary: Inca religion was the polytheist system of the Inca Empire, growing out of older Andean traditions and officially centred on the cult of the Sun, with Viracocha as creator and sacred places called wak'a. Cusco's panacas served its shrines and cared for the royal mummies, and human sacrifice took place in times of trouble.
notes: Dates: the article gives no founding date and no end date. Start 1200 (circa) and end 1559 are my placeholders; 1559 is the only year the article states (Polo de Ondegardo). The article does not say the religion ended; it notes Pachamama still figures in Bolivian belief. Please set start and end from another source or decide how to treat them.

Key events: the article dates almost nothing, so five of six labels are not years (Before the Inca, Inca Empire, Pachacutic's reign, Civil war, Spanish conquest). They will not sit on the timeline properly; the editor should add years from elsewhere or drop them.

Left out: the article's account of the triad of Viracocha, Inti and Inti-Illapa, and the two theories on why Viracocha rose above Inti (they are speculative and partly contradict the statement that Inti was the original most powerful god); Kon (Wakon) because the text is general; Mama Ocllo as regent; the story of Washkar's mother marrying his father's mummy; the claim that the Inca thought Spaniards god-like; the Tiwanaku hypothesis is kept as a hypothesis. The article spells names variably (Viracocha, Wiraqocha, Pacha Kuti/Pachacutic, Cusco/Cuzco, huaca/wak'a, Washkar/Huascar).

The article's 'Spanish conquest' dating is absent; Garcilaso is quoted on the preserved mummies but I kept only that he saw them. The article says Mamaquilla's temples were worked on by priestesses and that the Coya was 'considered the daughter of Mamaquilla'; omitted for length.

Faith map: all place names beyond Cusco, Lake Titicaca and Lima are the article's; coordinates from general geography. The article gives no dates for areas, so all areas start at 1200 (start) and the routes are limited to the 1559 transfer of the mummies to Lima.
